What is Data Science?
• Definition: Data Science is the process of using data, statistics, programming, 
and analytical techniques to discover useful information and support 
decision-making.
• Example: An online shopping website analyzes customer data to understand 
customer preferences, recommend products, and predict future purchases.

What is Data?
• Definition: Data is a collection of facts, observations, measurements, 
or information that can be used for analysis.
• Examples: Student marks, student name, temperature, photograph, 
video, customer review, transaction record.
• Student Data – Name, Attendance, and Marks.

Types of Data
Data can be broadly classified into:
1. Structured Data – Organized in a fixed format.
2. Semi-Structured Data – Has some organizational structure but does 
not follow a strict table format.
3. Unstructured Data – Does not have a predefined structure.
• Examples: 
• Structured → Database tables; 
• Semi-structured → JSON, XML; 
• Unstructured → Images, Videos, Audio.

Structured Data
• Meaning: Structured data is data organized in a fixed format, usually 
in rows and columns.
• Examples: Student database, employee records, bank transactions, 
sales records.
• Example fields: Student ID, Name, Marks.
• Common Storage: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Excel.

Semi-Structured Data
• Meaning: Semi-structured data does not follow a strict table structure 
but contains tags, keys, or labels that organize the information.
• Examples: JSON, XML, HTML, Emails.
• It is more flexible than structured data.

Unstructured Data
• Meaning: Unstructured data does not follow a predefined format or 
structure.
• Examples: Images, videos, audio files, text documents, social media 
posts, emails, online reviews.
• Example: A YouTube video contains video, audio, text, and comments. 
All these can become sources of data for analysis.

Data Sources
• What is a Data Source? A data source is a place or system from which 
data is collected.
• Major Data Sources: Databases; APIs; Websites and Web; Sensors 
and IoT devices; Social Media; Surveys and Forms; Government/Open 
Data; Cloud Platforms.
• Data Flow: Data Source → Data Collection → Data Storage → Data 
Analysis → Insights.

Databases
• What is a Database? A database is an organized collection of data that 
allows users to store, manage, and retrieve information.
• Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, 
MongoDB.
• Example: A college database may store student details, attendance, 
examination marks, course information, and faculty information.

APIs
• What is an API? API = Application Programming Interface.
• An API allows one software application to communicate with another 
application or service.
• Examples: Weather API, Google Maps API, Payment APIs, Social 
Media APIs.
• Example Flow: Application → API Request → Data Server → API 
Response → Application.

Websites and Web Data
• Websites contain large amounts of publicly available information.
• Examples: News websites, E-commerce websites, Educational 
websites, Job portals, Product review websites.
• Data Collection Methods: Web forms, APIs, Web scraping.
• Example: An e-commerce company can analyze product reviews to 
understand customer opinions.

Sensors and IoT
• IoT = Internet of Things.
• IoT devices collect data from the physical environment using sensors.
• Examples: Smart watches, fitness trackers, smart homes, traffic sensors, 
weather stations, industrial machines.
• Example: A fitness tracker collects steps, heart rate, sleep, and activity 
data.

Social Media
• Social media platforms generate huge amounts of data.
• Examples of Data: Posts, comments, likes, shares, images, videos, user 
profiles.
• Applications: Customer sentiment analysis, trend analysis, marketing, 
brand monitoring.
• Example: A company analyzes customer comments to understand 
whether customers are satisfied with a product.

Surveys and Forms
• Organizations often collect data directly from people using surveys, 
questionnaires, feedback forms, online forms, and interviews.
• Examples: Student satisfaction surveys, teaching feedback, course feedback, 
customer satisfaction, product feedback, market research.
• Popular Tools: Google Forms, Microsoft Forms, Survey platforms.

Government and Open Data
• Governments and public organizations provide datasets for public use.
• Examples: Population data, census data, weather data, economic data, 
education statistics, healthcare statistics, transportation data.
• Benefits: Research, policy analysis, public services, academic projects, 
data-driven decision-making.
• Example: Researchers can use government education data to study 
literacy trends.

Cloud Platforms
• Cloud platforms provide online infrastructure for storing and processing large 
amounts of data.
• Examples: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
• Cloud Data Sources: Cloud databases, cloud storage, application logs, 
business applications.
• Advantages: Scalable, accessible from anywhere, large storage capacity, 
supports large-scale data processing.

Examples of Data Sources
• Education → College Database → Marks, attendance
• Healthcare → Hospital System → Patient records
• Banking → Transaction Database → Transactions
• E-commerce → Website → Products, orders
• Social Media → Social Platforms → Posts, comments
• IoT → Sensors → Temperature
• Government → Open Data → Census data
• Transport → GPS/IoT → Vehicle location
• Key Idea: Different problems require different data sources.

Primary vs. Secondary Data
• Primary Data: Collected directly by the researcher; original data; surveys and 
interviews; experiments; questionnaires; more specific to the research 
problem.
• Secondary Data: Collected by someone else; existing data; government 
reports; research papers; public datasets; may already be available.
• Example: Primary Data – You conduct a survey of 500 students.
• Example: Secondary Data – You use an existing government education 
dataset.

Data Science Life Cycle
• The Data Science Life Cycle is a series of steps followed to solve a problem using data.
• Main Stages:
1. Business/Problem Understanding
2. Data Collection
3. Data Preparation
4. Exploratory Data Analysis
5. Feature Engineering
6. Model Building
7. Model Evaluation
8. Deployment
9. Monitoring and Maintenance
• Important: The process is iterative, meaning we may return to an earlier step when 
required.

Business/Problem Understanding
• Goal: Clearly understand the problem that needs to be solved.
• Activities: Define the problem; understand the objectives; identify users or 
stakeholders; define success criteria.
• Example Problem: Can we identify students who may need academic 
support?
• Goal: Predict students who may be at risk of poor academic performance.

Data Collection and Data Preparation
• Step 1: Data Collection – Collect relevant data from databases, APIs, surveys, 
websites, sensors, and open datasets.
• Step 2: Data Preparation – Remove duplicate records, handle missing values, 
correct errors, and convert data into suitable formats.
• Simple Flow: Raw Data → Cleaning → Transformation → Prepared Data.

Exploratory Data Analysis and Feature 
Engineering
• Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) helps us understand the data.
• EDA Activities: Calculate summary statistics, create graphs and charts, 
identify patterns, find relationships, detect unusual values.
• Feature Engineering: Features are useful attributes used for analysis or model 
building.
• Example: From Internal Marks, Semester Marks, and Attendance, we can 
create Average Marks and Attendance Percentage.

Model Building and Evaluation
• Model Building: Select an appropriate method and train a model using prepared 
data.
• Examples: Linear Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, Naive Bayes, 
Random Forest.
• Model Evaluation: Check how well the model performs.
• Common Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Mean Squared Error.
• Goal: Select a model that performs well on unseen data.

Deployment, Monitoring and Maintenance
• Deployment: Make the model available for actual use.
• Example: A college application predicts whether a student may need academic 
support.
• Monitoring: Continuously check model performance, data quality, and changes in 
data patterns.
• Maintenance: Update the model, retrain with new data, fix problems, and improve 
performance.
• Key Idea: Deployment is not the end of the Data Science Life Cycle.

Data Cleaning
• Data cleaning is the process of identifying and correcting inaccurate, 
incomplete, duplicate, or inconsistent data.
• Common Problems:
• Missing Value – Age = ?
• Duplicate – Same student entered twice
• Incorrect Value – Age = 250
• Inconsistent Format – Mumbai / MUMBAI / mumbai
• Outlier – Salary = $10,000,000
• Goal: Improve the quality and reliability of data.

Handling Missing Values
A missing value occurs when
 information is not available.
Example:
Possible techniques:
1. Delete the record
2. Replace with Mean
3. Replace with Median
4. Replace with Mode
5. Forward/Backward Fill
6. Predict the missing value
Student Age Marks
A 20 75
B ? (Missing) 80
C 21 85
D ? (Missing) 70

Numerical: Mean Imputation
Suppose the ages are: 20, 21, 22, ?, 24
Calculate the mean of available values:
Mean = (20 + 21 + 22 + 24) / 4
Mean = 87 / 4 = 21.75
Therefore, the missing value is replaced with 21.75.
Final Data: 20, 21, 22, 21.75, 24
When to Use? 
Mean imputation is useful when data is approximately symmetric and 
does not contain extreme outliers.

Numerical: Median Imputation
• Consider: 10, 12, 14, ?, 100
• Sorted available values: 10, 12, 14, 100
• Median = (12 + 14) / 2 = 13
• Replace missing value with 13.
• Why Median? 
• The value 100 is an extreme value and can significantly increase the 
mean.
• Therefore, median is often preferred when data contains outliers or 
skewness.

Mode Imputation
• Mode is the value that occurs most frequently.
• Example: Red, Blue, Red, Green, Red, ?
Frequency:
• Red = 3
• Blue = 1
• Green = 1
Therefore, Mode = Red.
Replace the missing value with Red.
Commonly Used For: Categorical data, Gender, City, Product category, 
Education level.

Removing Duplicate Records
Suppose a dataset contains:
ID | Name | Marks
101 | Amit | 80
102 | Neha | 75
101 | Amit | 80
103 | Ravi | 90
Total records = 4
Duplicate records = 1
After removing duplicates: Clean records = 4 − 1 = 3
Final dataset contains: 101 Amit, 102 Neha, 103 Ravi

Noisy Data
• Noise: random error or variance in a measured variable
• Incorrect attribute values may be due to
• Faulty data collection instruments
• Data entry problems
• Data transmission problems
• Technology limitation
• Inconsistency in naming convention 
• Other data problems which require data cleaning
• Duplicate records
• Incomplete data
• Inconsistent data

How to Handle Noisy Data?
• Binning
• First sort data and partition into (equal-frequency) bins
• Then one can smooth by bin means, smooth by bin median, smooth by bin 
boundaries, etc.
• Regression
• Smooth by fitting the data into regression functions
• Clustering
• Detect and remove outliers
• Combined Computer and Human Inspection
• Detect suspicious values and check by human (e.g., deal with possible outliers)

Simple Discretization: Binning
• Equal-width (distance) partitioning
• Divides the range into N intervals of equal size: uniform grid
• if A and B are the lowest and highest values of the attribute, the width of 
intervals will be: W = (B –A)/N.
• The most straightforward, but outliers may dominate presentation
• Skewed data is not handled well
• Equal-depth (frequency) partitioning
• Divides the range into N intervals, each containing approximately same number 
of samples
• Good data scaling

Data Transformation
Data transformation converts data from one format or scale into another 
format suitable for analysis.
Common Techniques:
• Normalization
• Standardization
• Encoding
• Aggregation
• Log Transformation
Example: Original values 10, 20, 30, 40 can be transformed using normalization 
to values between 0 and 1

Data Transformation 
• A function that maps the entire set of values of a given attribute to a 
new set of replacement values s.t. each old value can be identified 
with one of the new values
• Normalization: Scaled to fall within a smaller, specified range
• Min-Max normalization
• Z-Score normalization
• Normalization by decimal scaling

Min-Max Normalization
Min-Max normalization converts values into a fixed range, usually 0 to 1.
Formula: X' = (X − Xmin) / (Xmax
 − Xmin)
Notation Meaning
X Original value of the data point (before scaling).
X' Normalized (scaled) value after applying Min-Max scaling.
Xmin Minimum value of the feature (column) in the dataset.
X
max Maximum value of the feature (column) in the dataset.
(Xmax
 − Xmin) Range of the feature (difference between maximum and 
minimum values).

Eg: Let income range $12,000 to $98,000 normalized to [0.0, 1.0].  Then 
$73,600 is mapped to  ………….

Z-score normalization
Formula: Z = (X − μ) / σ
Where:
• X = Individual value
• μ = Mean
• σ = Standard deviation
Example: X = 80, Mean = 70, Standard deviation = 10
Z = (80 − 70) / 10 = 1
Answer: Z-score = 1

Data Integration
“Combines data from multiple sources into a coherent store.”
• Schema integration: e.g., A.cust-id ≡ B.cust#
• Integrate metadata from different sources
• Entity identification problem: 
• Identify real world entities from multiple data sources, e.g., customer_id in one 
database and cust_no in another database.
• Detecting and resolving data value conflicts
• For the same real world entity, attribute values from different sources are different
• Possible reasons: different representations, different scales
•  e.g., metric vs. British units

Data reduction
Data Reduction is the process of reducing the size, volume, or complexity of a 
dataset while preserving useful information.
Why Data Reduction?
• Reduces storage
• Speeds analysis
• Improves model performance
• Removes redundant data
• Reduces computation
• Simplifies visualization

• Data Cube Aggregation 
• Dimensionality Reduction 
• Data Compression 
• Numerosity Reduction
• Feature Selection 
• Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Techniques of Data Reduction

• Data Cube Aggregation summarizes detailed data into higher-level 
information.

• Dimensionality reduction decreases the number of attributes 
(columns) in the dataset.

Sampling
Obtaining a small sample s to represent the whole data set N
Types of Sampling
• Simple random sampling
• There is an equal probability of selecting any particular item
• Sampling without replacement
• Once an object is selected, it is removed from the population
• Sampling with replacement
• A selected object is not removed from the population(recorded and replaced)
• Stratified sampling: 
• Partition the data set, and draw samples from each partition (proportionally, 
i.e., approximately the same percentage of the data) 
• Used in conjunction with skewed data

Discretization 
“Divide the range of a continuous attribute into intervals”
• Interval labels can then be used to replace actual data values 
• Reduce data size by discretization.
• Supervised vs. unsupervised.
• Split (top-down) vs. merge (bottom-up).
• Discretization can be performed recursively on an attribute.
• Prepare for further analysis, e.g., classification.

Measuring the Dispersion of Data
• Quantiles :are points taken at regular intervals of a data distribution, dividing it into 
essentially equal size consecutive sets
• The 2-quantile is the data point dividing the lower and upper halves of the data 
distribution
• The 4-quantiles are the three data points that split the data distribution into four 
equal parts; each part represents one-fourth of the data distribution. 
• They are more commonly referred to as quartiles
• The 100-quantiles are more commonly referred to as percentiles; they divide the 
data distribution into 100 equal-sized consecutive sets
• Quartiles: Q1
 (25th percentile), Q3
 (75th percentile)
• Inter-quartile range: IQR = Q3 – Q1

Boxplot Analysis
• Five-number summary of a distribution
• Minimum, Q1, Median, Q3, Maximum
• Boxplot
• Data is represented with a box.
• The ends of the box are at the first and third quartiles, i.e., the height of the 
box is IQR
• The median is marked by a line within the box
• Whiskers: two lines outside the box extended to Minimum and Maximum
• Outliers: points beyond a specified outlier threshold, plotted individually

Approaches to Data visualization
• Pixel-oriented techniques
• Geometric projection techniques
• Icon-based techniques
• Hierarchical and graph-based techniques

Pixel-oriented techniques
Definition
Each data value is represented by 
a colored pixel. Similar values are 
assigned similar colors.
Applications
• Very large datasets 
• High-dimensional 
visualization 
• Pattern recognition

Icon-Based Visualization
Each data object is represented by an 
icon (glyph), and attribute values are 
mapped to visual features such as size, 
shape, orientation, or color.
Example
• Star plots 
• Chernoff faces 
Applications
• Multidimensional data visualization 
• Pattern comparison

Geometric Projection Visualization
High-dimensional data is projected 
into two or three dimensions for 
visualization while preserving 
important relationships.
Applications
• Cluster visualization 
• Dimension reduction 
• Pattern discovery

Hierarchical Visualization
Data is visualized using a 
hierarchical structure.
Examples
• Tree maps 
• Cone trees 
Applications
• Hierarchical datasets 
• File systems 
• Organizational structures

Graph-Based Visualization
Definition
Objects are represented as 
nodes, and relationships 
between objects are represented 
as edges.
Applications
• Social networks 
• Transportation networks 
• Web page links 
• Recommendation systems
